screens.title: Threat Detection with Flexible NetFlow and IP SLA
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will understand how two complementary Cisco features — Flexible NetFlow and IP Service Level Agreements — work together to detect network threats and protect service availability. Flexible NetFlow gives you deep, customizable visibility into traffic flows so you can spot anomalies like spikes to a destination port or scanning behavior. IP SLA actively probes services to measure reachability, latency, and jitter, alerting you to degradation that could signal an attack or outage. Together they let you detect an incident and automate a response, for example by withdrawing a route when a monitored server becomes unreachable. You will also see concrete configuration examples: how to define a security-focused flow record and exporter, apply a flow monitor to an interface, and how to create an IP SLA ICMP operation tied to a tracking object. A common pitfall is collecting too many fields or probing too frequently — both can overload a device. As you explore, think about what minimal fields and probe frequencies would answer your threat-detection questions without harming performance. By the end of the lesson you will be able to configure FNF and IP SLA for practical threat detection and tie them together for automated failover. What minimal set of measurements would you choose first on your border router?

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Part 1)
screens.narratorSegment: In the first set of objectives we focus on understanding Flexible NetFlow and the basics of IP SLA configuration. You will explain the role of Flexible NetFlow for visibility and threat detection, learning how customizable flow records let you capture the fields most relevant to security investigations. You will practice configuring Flexible NetFlow to capture specific traffic parameters and export them to a NetFlow collector, so data appears where analysts can examine it. You will analyze NetFlow data to identify anomalies, such as sudden spikes or scanning behavior, and learn the signs of DoS, worms, or insider data exfiltration. Finally, you will describe the capabilities of IP Service Level Agreements for proactive network monitoring and how they surface service degradation before users complain. Each objective is framed for hands-on practice: start with one flow record and one IP SLA probe, verify results, then scale. This approach helps you avoid common mistakes like over-collecting fields or probing too frequently, which can degrade device performance. As you move through the exercises, think about which fields and probe types would answer your most pressing security questions.

screens.title: What is Flexible NetFlow (FNF)?
screens.narratorSegment: Flexible NetFlow is a customizable, scalable technology for collecting telemetry about traffic flows that goes beyond the fixed field sets of legacy NetFlow. At its core FNF lets you define flow records that specify keys used to identify a flow — for example source address, destination address, transport ports, and protocol — and non-key fields to collect additional context such as packet and byte counters or TCP flags. That flexibility matters for security: you can target the fields that reveal attack patterns, like a sudden burst of packets to a single destination port or repeated SYNs without completion. A concrete example is a security-focused flow record that matches IPv4 protocol, source and destination addresses, source and destination ports, and collects TCP flags plus byte and packet counters. This record gives you the minimal view to detect a UDP flood, scanning activity, or odd TCP flag patterns associated with reconnaissance. A common misconception is that more fields always equal better visibility. In practice, collecting too many fields increases C P U and memory use and can overwhelm both the device and your collector. Start with the fields needed to answer your security questions, verify you can export and parse the data, then expand cautiously. The key takeaway is that FNF gives you surgical visibility: pick the right fields, apply monitors only where required, and validate exporter throughput before scaling.

keyIdea.title: FNF in one line
keyIdea.text: Flexible NetFlow lets you define exactly what flow data to capture so security teams can detect and investigate anomalies.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Flexible NetFlow (FNF)?
Customizable flow telemetry for deep network visibility.
Definition & why it matters

Flexible NetFlow allows you to define records of key and non-key fields. Keys identify unique flows; non-keys add counters and context. This tailoring helps you capture only the telemetry you need to detect security patterns without excessive overhead.

Analogy
Think of FNF as choosing which camera angles and sensors you want in a security room. Too many feeds overload operators; the right feeds show the incident clearly.
Common misconception
More fields automatically equals better detection. Not true — collect what you need and monitor resource usage.
Concrete example: security record
flow record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
 match ipv4 protocol
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 collect transport tcp flags
 collect counter bytes long
 collect counter packets long
Use
Detect floods, scanning, and TCP-flag anomalies.
Monitor
Verify flow cache and exporter counters after enabling.
Key Takeaway

Define minimal, security-focused records and scale only after validating resource impact.

screens.title: FNF Components: Record, Exporter, Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Flexible NetFlow is built from three collaborating components: flow record, flow exporter, and flow monitor. The flow record defines what to observe — the keys to identify a flow and non-key fields to collect counters or flags. The flow exporter defines where telemetry is sent, usually the IP and UDP port of a NetFlow collector, plus the source interface for packets. The flow monitor binds a record to an exporter and manages an on-device cache that aggregates flow entries before export. When you apply the flow monitor to an interface in the input or output direction, the device populates the cache with flows matching the record and periodically exports them to the configured collector. A concrete configuration pattern is to create a security record matching protocol and addresses, configure an exporter with the collector IP and UDP 2055, then create a monitor that references both and set a cache timeout of 60 seconds. A common operational mistake is applying a monitor that collects many fields on many high-throughput interfaces; this can exhaust memory and increase C P U for flow processing and export. To be safe, start by applying the monitor to a single interface handling the traffic you want to inspect, verify export statistics and cache entries with show commands, and then expand to additional interfaces or richer records only after validating performance. Remember: the monitor is the operational binding; the exporter is the delivery channel; the record is the telemetry schema. That separation lets you reuse the same record with different exporters or apply different records to different interfaces as needed.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Records define telemetry, exporters choose the collector and transport, monitors bind schema to export and are applied to interfaces.

content.html:
Definition
FNF Components: Record, Exporter, Monitor
Three distinct layers let you control what to collect, where to send it, and how it runs on the device.
Component Overview
Flow Record: Defines keys (e.g., IPv4 source/destination, ports) and non-keys (counters, TCP flags).
Flow Exporter: Destination IP, transport UDP port, and source interface for NetFlow packets.
Flow Monitor: Associates a record and exporter and manages the flow cache for export.
Operational tip
Apply monitors to only the interfaces you need and use short cache timeouts for security-focused export rates.
Combined configuration pattern
flow record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
 record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
  match ipv4 protocol
  match ipv4 source address
  match ipv4 destination address
  match transport source-port
  match transport destination-port
  collect transport tcp flags
  collect counter bytes long
  collect counter packets long
!
flow exporter FNF_EXPORTER
 destination 192.168.10.30
 transport udp 2055
 source GigabitEthernet0/0/0
!
flow monitor FNF_MONITOR
 record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
 exporter FNF_EXPORTER
 cache timeout active 60
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip flow monitor FNF_MONITOR input
 ip flow monitor FNF_MONITOR output
Verify
Use show flow monitor <name> cache and statistics to validate collection and export.
Watchout
Avoid wide application on many interfaces; monitor device CPU and memory after enabling.

screens.title: Configure a Security-Focused Flow Record
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a configuration you will use repeatedly when you want to detect attacks. The goal is to capture fields that reveal scanning, floods, and unusual connection patterns while minimizing device load. Start by creating a flow record that matches the IPv4 protocol, source and destination addresses, and transport source and destination ports. Add collect statements for TCP flags and counters for bytes and packets. These counters let you detect sudden byte or packet spikes; TCP flags let you see half-open SYN floods. After you create the record, define a flow exporter pointing to your NetFlow collector using UDP port 2055 and pick a stable source interface such as a loopback. Then bind the record and exporter with a flow monitor and set a reasonable cache timeout, for example 60 seconds, so data is exported frequently enough for timely detection but not so often it raises overhead. A frequent misconception is to put every possible field into the record. That yields large flow entries which use more memory and increase processing time. Instead, begin with this security-focused set, apply the monitor to the targeted interface, and run show flow monitor cache and statistics to confirm you are receiving usable flows at the collector. If your collector shows meaningful alerts, you can incrementally add fields such as AS numbers or QoS markings as needed.

keyIdea.title: Start focused
keyIdea.text: Begin with a minimal security-focused record; expand fields only after validating export and device performance.

content.html:
Process Flow
Configure a Security-Focused Flow Record
A step-by-step code walkthrough to capture attacker-revealing fields.
Configuration snippet
flow record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
 match ipv4 protocol
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 collect transport tcp flags
 collect counter bytes long
 collect counter packets long
Why each field:
  • Protocol identifies UDP vs TCP floods or ICMP probes.
  • Addresses and ports pinpoint target servers and services.
  • TCP flags reveal incomplete handshakes or suspicious flag combos.
  • Counters show volume and connection rates for DoS detection.
Practical checklist
Apply to only internal interfaces you monitor for threats.
Set cache timeout to balance detection speed with resource use.
Avoid overly broad records that include rare fields unless required for a use case.
Key Takeaway

A focused flow record provides the best signal-to-noise ratio for security detection while protecting device resources.

screens.title: Define Exporter, Monitor, and Apply to Interface
screens.narratorSegment: After you define what to collect, you need to deliver it to a collector and enable collection on interfaces. The flow exporter specifies the collector IP, transport UDP port, and the source interface for export packets. Typically you use UDP 2055 and a loopback or physical interface as the source so the export source stays consistent. The flow monitor references the record and exporter and sets a cache timeout that controls export frequency. Finally, apply the monitor to an interface in the input or output direction. A concrete example uses an exporter destination of 192.168.10.30 with transport UDP 2055, source GigabitEthernet0/0/0, and a monitor with cache timeout active 60. Apply ip flow monitor input and output to the interface you want to inspect. Once enabled, verify collection with show flow monitor cache to see current flow entries, and show flow monitor statistics to confirm export packets are sent. A misconception is thinking the exporter must be unique per monitor; exporters can be reused by multiple monitors if they send to the same collector. Also, beware of source-interface selection: using a loopback ensures a consistent source but requires that the loopback is routable to the collector. Plan the routing so export packets reach the collector reliably. Validate the collector receives and parses flows before expanding coverage.

keyIdea.title: Activation steps
keyIdea.text: Exporters send telemetry, monitors manage cache and export timing, and applying monitors to interfaces enables flow capture.

content.html:
Process Flow
Define Exporter, Monitor, and Apply to Interface
From exporter to interface: ensure delivery and activation of flow data.
Exporter + Monitor snippet
flow exporter FNF_EXPORTER
 destination 192.168.10.30
 transport udp 2055
 source GigabitEthernet0/0/0
!
flow monitor FNF_MONITOR
 record FNF_SECURITY_RECORD
 exporter FNF_EXPORTER
 cache timeout active 60
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip flow monitor FNF_MONITOR input
 ip flow monitor FNF_MONITOR output
Verification commands
  • show flow monitor FNF_MONITOR cache
  • show flow monitor FNF_MONITOR statistics
  • confirm collector is receiving exported records
Operational notes
Use a loopback as exporter source for consistent source IPs, and ensure the loopback is routable to the collector.
Re-use exporters for multiple monitors if they share the same destination to reduce config duplication.
Monitor CPU and memory after enabling; scale slowly across interfaces.
Key Takeaway

Confirm both device-side statistics and collector ingestion before scaling FNF across many interfaces.

screens.title: Detecting Threats with NetFlow Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: NetFlow data reveals behavioral signatures that are useful for detecting a variety of security incidents. For a DoS or DDoS event, you often see sudden spikes in packets or bytes directed to a single destination or destination port, and a high connection or request rate from one or many source addresses. For scanning or worm propagation, flows show many small connections or connection attempts to sequential destination ports or many destination addresses from a single source. Malware and command-and-control communications may appear as regular, persistent flows to external IPs at unusual ports; correlating flows with DNS or known bad IPs helps confirm suspicion. Insider threats can be visible as abnormal east-west flows or large data transfers to destinations that normally have little traffic. Policy violations appear when flows exist on segments where those services should be blocked. A concrete example: if you see match transport destination-port and match ipv4 destination address fields showing a sudden high packet and byte count to port 445 on a server, this could indicate a targeted SMB flood or worm. Always cross-validate flow anomalies with other telemetry like syslogs, IDS alerts, or packet captures before concluding an attack. A common misconception is that NetFlow alone proves malicious intent; NetFlow is evidence of behavior patterns that need further context. The takeaway is that properly designed flow records let you detect patterns quickly and then escalate to deeper inspection when needed.

keyIdea.title: Flow patterns matter
keyIdea.text: Specific flow signatures — spikes, many small flows, repeated external contacts — map to different threat scenarios and guide escalation.

content.html:
Comparison
Detecting Threats with NetFlow Patterns
Map flow characteristics to likely security incidents.
DoS / DDoS
Sudden increase in bytes/packets to one destination or destination port; many source IPs or one source with high packet rate. Use counters to spot volume and connection-rate anomalies.
Worms / Scanning
Many short-lived flows to many destinations or many destination ports from the same source indicate scanning or propagation activity.
Insider Data Exfiltration
Unusual large transfers to external hosts or east-west transfers to storage segments warrant investigation.
Policy Violations
Flows on restricted segments or to blocked services should not exist; their presence indicates misconfiguration or violation.
Concrete detection example
Observed: destination 10.1.1.5 port 445, packets 1,200,000 in 60s
Interpretation: potential SMB flood or worm activity — escalate to packet capture and containment.
Cross-check flows with DNS logs, IDS alerts, or packet captures before taking automated containment actions.

screens.title: What is IP SLA?
screens.narratorSegment: IP Service Level Agreements are active probes a Cisco device generates to test the performance and reachability of network services. Unlike passive telemetry, IP SLA actively creates traffic — such as ICMP echo, UDP jitter for VoIP-like measurements, TCP connect to test application ports, or HTTP GET for web response times — and records metrics like round-trip time, jitter, and packet loss. These operations help detect Denial-of-Service attacks where latency or packet loss rises, service outages where probes fail entirely, and performance degradation that could hint at a compromised server or network congestion. You configure an IP SLA operation with an operation ID, destination, source interface, timeout, and frequency, then schedule it to run continuously. The true security power comes from linking IP SLA to a tracking object. If a probe fails, the tracking object changes state and can be referenced by static routes or routing protocols to withdraw a path or trigger an alternate. A common misconfiguration is using probe frequencies that are too aggressive — this can overwhelm the device and produce false positives. Balance probe frequency and timeout to minimize load while still detecting meaningful changes. Use IP SLA proactively: it provides a synthetic heartbeat for critical services so you can act before users report an outage.

keyIdea.title: IP SLA in one line
keyIdea.text: IP SLA actively probes services to measure reachability and performance and can trigger automated responses via tracking objects.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is IP SLA?
Active probes that simulate traffic to measure service health and performance.
Operation types
  • ICMP Echo: round-trip time and packet loss.
  • UDP Jitter: one-way delay, jitter, loss for VoIP checks.
  • TCP Connect: time to establish a TCP connection to a port.
  • HTTP GET: web server response time.
Use the operation type that most closely simulates the service you want to protect. An ICMP probe measures reachability but may not expose application-level issues that a TCP connect or HTTP GET would reveal.
Best practice
Choose probe frequency and timeout that represent the service without overloading the device. Integrate with tracking to create automated routing or alerting behavior when a probe fails.
Key Takeaway

IP SLA provides a synthetic check of service health that can drive automated network decisions when configured with tracking objects.

screens.title: Configure IP SLA and Schedule It
screens.narratorSegment: We'll configure an IP SLA operation to monitor a critical server's reachability using ICMP echo. Start with ip sla 10, then specify icmp-echo with the destination IP and a source-interface, for example a loopback. Set timeout and frequency so probes run every five seconds with a 2-second timeout. After defining the operation, schedule it to run forever starting now using ip sla schedule. This keeps continuous measurements so you can detect latency increases or loss quickly. For security, frequent probes can highlight DoS impacts but can themselves increase device load — choose a frequency that balances visibility and overhead. Verification commands include show ip sla summary to check operation status and show ip sla detail 10 for per-operation metrics. Use these to see RTT and packet loss reported by the device. Once the operation is running and reporting, you can link it to a tracking object so its up/down state can influence routing. A common mistake is scheduling many high-frequency probes on the same device; instead, monitor critical paths and scale probes across devices thoughtfully. The immediate benefit is a live indicator of service health that complements passive flow analysis by providing an active measurement of service reachability and performance.

Process Flow
Configure IP SLA and Schedule It
An ICMP example and verification steps.
Configuration example
ip sla 10
 icmp-echo 192.168.1.100 source-interface Loopback0
 timeout 2000
 frequency 5
!
ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now
Verification
  • show ip sla summary
  • show ip sla detail 10
Operational guidance
Use Loopback0 as the source for consistent probe source addresses and to simplify routing to the monitored destination.
A reasonable frequency (for example 5 seconds) balances timeliness and device load; adjust for your environment.

A scheduled IP SLA operation provides continuous performance metrics you can use for alerting and automated responses.

screens.title: Tracking Objects and Automated Failover
screens.narratorSegment: Tracking objects convert the result of an IP SLA operation into a boolean state that other features can use. When you configure track 1 ip sla 10 reachability, the tracking object becomes 'up' when the IP SLA operation succeeds and 'down' when it fails. You can reference that tracking object from a static route so the route is installed only when the tracked operation is up, or removed when the operation fails. For example, a static host route to a critical server can be configured with track 1 so traffic follows the primary path only when the IP SLA probe confirms reachability. This mechanism provides automated failover without manual intervention. A concrete configuration pattern: create IP SLA 10 to probe the server, schedule it, create track 1 ip sla 10 reachability, and add ip route 192.168.1.100 255.255.255.255 192.168.1.1 track 1. Verify the track state using show track 1 and observe the static route presence with show ip route 192.168.1.100. A misconception is to assume tracking prevents attacks; it only automates network behavior based on reachability and performance. Use it to preserve service availability and route around failures, but combine with flow analysis and security controls for full threat mitigation. Test the behaviour by simulating server failure and observing the tracker and route reaction to confirm the automation works as intended.

Tracking Objects and Automated Failover
Use tracking state to conditionally install or withdraw routes and automate responses to probe failures.
Configuration snippet

!

screens.title: Hands-on Scenario: R1 Configuration Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This scenario walks you through a practical implementation on router R1. The objectives are to enable Flexible NetFlow on the internal interface, export to a collector sourced from Loopback0, and configure an IP SLA probe tied to a tracking object that conditions a static route. Begin by creating Loopback0 with an address to use as the flow-export source. Then create the FNF record, exporter pointing to 192.168.10.40 UDP 2055 with source Loopback0, and a monitor that references the record and exporter with a 60 second active cache timeout. Apply the monitor input and output to GigabitEthernet0/0/1 where your internal LAN attaches. Next, configure ip sla 10 with icmp-echo to 192.168.1.100 sourced from Loopback0, set timeout 2000 and frequency 5, then schedule it. Create track 1 ip sla 10 reachability and add a static host route to 192.168.1.100 that uses track 1 to be active only when the probe reports reachability. After committing the configuration, verify collection using show flow monitor FNF_MONITOR cache and statistics, confirm IP SLA with show ip sla summary and show ip sla detail 10, check the tracking object with show track 1, and confirm the static route presence with show ip route 192.168.1.100. Then simulate a server failure by shutting the server interface and watch the track state change and the static route withdraw. This test validates both detection and automated response.

Hands-on Activity
Hands-on Scenario: R1 Configuration Walkthrough
Implement FNF and IP SLA together on a border router and verify detection and automated response.
R1 Configuration (concise)
enable
configure terminal

interface Loopback0

! Step 1: Configure Flexible NetFlow

 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Operational Safeguards
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring operational mistakes that can turn powerful tools into problems if not avoided. First, collecting too many fields in Flexible NetFlow or applying monitors to many high-throughput interfaces can exhaust C P U and memory. The safeguard is to start with essential fields and test on a single interface, monitor resource use, and then expand. Second, setting IP SLA probe frequencies too high can create false positives and impose extra load; choose timeouts and frequencies that reflect the service without flooding the device. Third, using inappropriate probe targets — for example, pinging an address that is not representative of the user-facing service — can produce misleading results. Make sure the monitored destination accurately represents the service experience. Fourth, assuming NetFlow alone proves malicious intent is a mistake: flows indicate behavior patterns and must be correlated with logs, IDS alerts, or packet captures before decisive action. Finally, misconfiguring exporter source interfaces can cause exports to fail if the source is not routable to the collector; use loopbacks or ensure routing is correct. The practical safeguard is a staged rollout with verification steps: configure, verify show outputs and collector ingestion, simulate failures, and monitor device performance before scaling. These practices preserve detection capability while avoiding unintended outages or noisy telemetry.

Common Mistakes
Common Mistakes and Operational Safeguards
Practical checks to avoid overloads and false positives.
Too many FNF fields
Collecting every field increases flow entry size and device overhead. Start minimal and expand later.
High-frequency probes
Probing too often can create false positives and consume CPU. Choose a balanced frequency.
Unrepresentative targets
Ensure the IP SLA destination reflects the real service endpoint, not just a reachable network device.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will understand how two complementary Cisco features — Flexible NetFlow and IP Service Level Agreements — work together to detect network threats and protect service availability. Flexible NetFlow gives you deep, customizable visibility into traffic flows so you can spot anomalies like spikes to a destination port or scanning behavior. IP SLA actively probes services to measure reachability, latency, and jitter, alerting you to degradation that could signal an attack or outage. Together they let you detect an incident and automate a response, for example by withdrawing a route when a monitored server becomes unreachable. You will also see concrete configuration examples: how to define a security-focused flow record and exporter, apply a flow monitor to an interface, and how to create an IP SLA ICMP operation tied to a tracking object. A common pitfall is collecting too many fields or probing too frequently — both can overload a device. As you explore, think about what minimal fields and probe frequencies would answer your threat-detection questions without harming performance. By the end of the lesson you will be able to configure FNF and IP SLA for practical threat detection and tie them together for automated failover. What minimal set of measurements would you choose first on your border router?

In the first set of objectives we focus on understanding Flexible NetFlow and the basics of IP SLA configuration. You will explain the role of Flexible NetFlow for visibility and threat detection, learning how customizable flow records let you capture the fields most relevant to security investigations. You will practice configuring Flexible NetFlow to capture specific traffic parameters and export them to a NetFlow collector, so data appears where analysts can examine it. You will analyze NetFlow data to identify anomalies, such as sudden spikes or scanning behavior, and learn the signs of DoS, worms, or insider data exfiltration. Finally, you will describe the capabilities of IP Service Level Agreements for proactive network monitoring and how they surface service degradation before users complain. Each objective is framed for hands-on practice: start with one flow record and one IP SLA probe, verify results, then scale. This approach helps you avoid common mistakes like over-collecting fields or probing too frequently, which can degrade device performance. As you move through the exercises, think about which fields and probe types would answer your most pressing security questions.

This second set of objectives focuses on hands-on IP SLA operations and integration with tracking for automated responses. You will configure various IP SLA operations — for example ICMP echo to measure round-trip time and UDP jitter to measure one-way delay and packet loss — so you can detect performance issues that may be caused by attacks or routing problems. You will integrate IP SLA with tracking objects and routing so that a probe failure can withdraw a route or trigger an alternate path, ensuring business continuity when a service is degraded or unreachable. You will also learn practical configuration safeguards: select probe frequency and timeouts that minimize false alarms and device load. Finally, you will practice verification commands to confirm both NetFlow export and IP SLA operation state. These skills let you combine passive flow analysis with active probing to detect anomalies early and automate recoveries without manual intervention.

Flexible NetFlow is a customizable, scalable technology for collecting telemetry about traffic flows that goes beyond the fixed field sets of legacy NetFlow. At its core FNF lets you define flow records that specify keys used to identify a flow — for example source address, destination address, transport ports, and protocol — and non-key fields to collect additional context such as packet and byte counters or TCP flags. That flexibility matters for security: you can target the fields that reveal attack patterns, like a sudden burst of packets to a single destination port or repeated SYNs without completion. A concrete example is a security-focused flow record that matches IPv4 protocol, source and destination addresses, source and destination ports, and collects TCP flags plus byte and packet counters. This record gives you the minimal view to detect a UDP flood, scanning activity, or odd TCP flag patterns associated with reconnaissance. A common misconception is that more fields always equal better visibility. In practice, collecting too many fields increases C P U and memory use and can overwhelm both the device and your collector. Start with the fields needed to answer your security questions, verify you can export and parse the data, then expand cautiously. The key takeaway is that FNF gives you surgical visibility: pick the right fields, apply monitors only where required, and validate exporter throughput before scaling.

Flexible NetFlow is built from three collaborating components: flow record, flow exporter, and flow monitor. The flow record defines what to observe — the keys to identify a flow and non-key fields to collect counters or flags. The flow exporter defines where telemetry is sent, usually the IP and UDP port of a NetFlow collector, plus the source interface for packets. The flow monitor binds a record to an exporter and manages an on-device cache that aggregates flow entries before export. When you apply the flow monitor to an interface in the input or output direction, the device populates the cache with flows matching the record and periodically exports them to the configured collector. A concrete configuration pattern is to create a security record matching protocol and addresses, configure an exporter with the collector IP and UDP 2055, then create a monitor that references both and set a cache timeout of 60 seconds. A common operational mistake is applying a monitor that collects many fields on many high-throughput interfaces; this can exhaust memory and increase C P U for flow processing and export. To be safe, start by applying the monitor to a single interface handling the traffic you want to inspect, verify export statistics and cache entries with show commands, and then expand to additional interfaces or richer records only after validating performance. Remember: the monitor is the operational binding; the exporter is the delivery channel; the record is the telemetry schema. That separation lets you reuse the same record with different exporters or apply different records to different interfaces as needed.

Let's walk through a configuration you will use repeatedly when you want to detect attacks. The goal is to capture fields that reveal scanning, floods, and unusual connection patterns while minimizing device load. Start by creating a flow record that matches the IPv4 protocol, source and destination addresses, and transport source and destination ports. Add collect statements for TCP flags and counters for bytes and packets. These counters let you detect sudden byte or packet spikes; TCP flags let you see half-open SYN floods. After you create the record, define a flow exporter pointing to your NetFlow collector using UDP port 2055 and pick a stable source interface such as a loopback. Then bind the record and exporter with a flow monitor and set a reasonable cache timeout, for example 60 seconds, so data is exported frequently enough for timely detection but not so often it raises overhead. A frequent misconception is to put every possible field into the record. That yields large flow entries which use more memory and increase processing time. Instead, begin with this security-focused set, apply the monitor to the targeted interface, and run show flow monitor cache and statistics to confirm you are receiving usable flows at the collector. If your collector shows meaningful alerts, you can incrementally add fields such as AS numbers or QoS markings as needed.

After you define what to collect, you need to deliver it to a collector and enable collection on interfaces. The flow exporter specifies the collector IP, transport UDP port, and the source interface for export packets. Typically you use UDP 2055 and a loopback or physical interface as the source so the export source stays consistent. The flow monitor references the record and exporter and sets a cache timeout that controls export frequency. Finally, apply the monitor to an interface in the input or output direction. A concrete example uses an exporter destination of 192.168.10.30 with transport UDP 2055, source GigabitEthernet0/0/0, and a monitor with cache timeout active 60. Apply ip flow monitor input and output to the interface you want to inspect. Once enabled, verify collection with show flow monitor cache to see current flow entries, and show flow monitor statistics to confirm export packets are sent. A misconception is thinking the exporter must be unique per monitor; exporters can be reused by multiple monitors if they send to the same collector. Also, beware of source-interface selection: using a loopback ensures a consistent source but requires that the loopback is routable to the collector. Plan the routing so export packets reach the collector reliably. Validate the collector receives and parses flows before expanding coverage.

NetFlow data reveals behavioral signatures that are useful for detecting a variety of security incidents. For a DoS or DDoS event, you often see sudden spikes in packets or bytes directed to a single destination or destination port, and a high connection or request rate from one or many source addresses. For scanning or worm propagation, flows show many small connections or connection attempts to sequential destination ports or many destination addresses from a single source. Malware and command-and-control communications may appear as regular, persistent flows to external IPs at unusual ports; correlating flows with DNS or known bad IPs helps confirm suspicion. Insider threats can be visible as abnormal east-west flows or large data transfers to destinations that normally have little traffic. Policy violations appear when flows exist on segments where those services should be blocked. A concrete example: if you see match transport destination-port and match ipv4 destination address fields showing a sudden high packet and byte count to port 445 on a server, this could indicate a targeted SMB flood or worm. Always cross-validate flow anomalies with other telemetry like syslogs, IDS alerts, or packet captures before concluding an attack. A common misconception is that NetFlow alone proves malicious intent; NetFlow is evidence of behavior patterns that need further context. The takeaway is that properly designed flow records let you detect patterns quickly and then escalate to deeper inspection when needed.

IP Service Level Agreements are active probes a Cisco device generates to test the performance and reachability of network services. Unlike passive telemetry, IP SLA actively creates traffic — such as ICMP echo, UDP jitter for VoIP-like measurements, TCP connect to test application ports, or HTTP GET for web response times — and records metrics like round-trip time, jitter, and packet loss. These operations help detect Denial-of-Service attacks where latency or packet loss rises, service outages where probes fail entirely, and performance degradation that could hint at a compromised server or network congestion. You configure an IP SLA operation with an operation ID, destination, source interface, timeout, and frequency, then schedule it to run continuously. The true security power comes from linking IP SLA to a tracking object. If a probe fails, the tracking object changes state and can be referenced by static routes or routing protocols to withdraw a path or trigger an alternate. A common misconfiguration is using probe frequencies that are too aggressive — this can overwhelm the device and produce false positives. Balance probe frequency and timeout to minimize load while still detecting meaningful changes. Use IP SLA proactively: it provides a synthetic heartbeat for critical services so you can act before users report an outage.

We'll configure an IP SLA operation to monitor a critical server's reachability using ICMP echo. Start with ip sla 10, then specify icmp-echo with the destination IP and a source-interface, for example a loopback. Set timeout and frequency so probes run every five seconds with a 2-second timeout. After defining the operation, schedule it to run forever starting now using ip sla schedule. This keeps continuous measurements so you can detect latency increases or loss quickly. For security, frequent probes can highlight DoS impacts but can themselves increase device load — choose a frequency that balances visibility and overhead. Verification commands include show ip sla summary to check operation status and show ip sla detail 10 for per-operation metrics. Use these to see RTT and packet loss reported by the device. Once the operation is running and reporting, you can link it to a tracking object so its up/down state can influence routing. A common mistake is scheduling many high-frequency probes on the same device; instead, monitor critical paths and scale probes across devices thoughtfully. The immediate benefit is a live indicator of service health that complements passive flow analysis by providing an active measurement of service reachability and performance.

Tracking objects convert the result of an IP SLA operation into a boolean state that other features can use. When you configure track 1 ip sla 10 reachability, the tracking object becomes 'up' when the IP SLA operation succeeds and 'down' when it fails. You can reference that tracking object from a static route so the route is installed only when the tracked operation is up, or removed when the operation fails. For example, a static host route to a critical server can be configured with track 1 so traffic follows the primary path only when the IP SLA probe confirms reachability. This mechanism provides automated failover without manual intervention. A concrete configuration pattern: create IP SLA 10 to probe the server, schedule it, create track 1 ip sla 10 reachability, and add ip route 192.168.1.100 255.255.255.255 192.168.1.1 track 1. Verify the track state using show track 1 and observe the static route presence with show ip route 192.168.1.100. A misconception is to assume tracking prevents attacks; it only automates network behavior based on reachability and performance. Use it to preserve service availability and route around failures, but combine with flow analysis and security controls for full threat mitigation. Test the behaviour by simulating server failure and observing the tracker and route reaction to confirm the automation works as intended.

This scenario walks you through a practical implementation on router R1. The objectives are to enable Flexible NetFlow on the internal interface, export to a collector sourced from Loopback0, and configure an IP SLA probe tied to a tracking object that conditions a static route. Begin by creating Loopback0 with an address to use as the flow-export source. Then create the FNF record, exporter pointing to 192.168.10.40 UDP 2055 with source Loopback0, and a monitor that references the record and exporter with a 60 second active cache timeout. Apply the monitor input and output to GigabitEthernet0/0/1 where your internal LAN attaches. Next, configure ip sla 10 with icmp-echo to 192.168.1.100 sourced from Loopback0, set timeout 2000 and frequency 5, then schedule it. Create track 1 ip sla 10 reachability and add a static host route to 192.168.1.100 that uses track 1 to be active only when the probe reports reachability. After committing the configuration, verify collection using show flow monitor FNF_MONITOR cache and statistics, confirm IP SLA with show ip sla summary and show ip sla detail 10, check the tracking object with show track 1, and confirm the static route presence with show ip route 192.168.1.100. Then simulate a server failure by shutting the server interface and watch the track state change and the static route withdraw. This test validates both detection and automated response.

There are recurring operational mistakes that can turn powerful tools into problems if not avoided. First, collecting too many fields in Flexible NetFlow or applying monitors to many high-throughput interfaces can exhaust C P U and memory. The safeguard is to start with essential fields and test on a single interface, monitor resource use, and then expand. Second, setting IP SLA probe frequencies too high can create false positives and impose extra load; choose timeouts and frequencies that reflect the service without flooding the device. Third, using inappropriate probe targets — for example, pinging an address that is not representative of the user-facing service — can produce misleading results. Make sure the monitored destination accurately represents the service experience. Fourth, assuming NetFlow alone proves malicious intent is a mistake: flows indicate behavior patterns and must be correlated with logs, IDS alerts, or packet captures before decisive action. Finally, misconfiguring exporter source interfaces can cause exports to fail if the source is not routable to the collector; use loopbacks or ensure routing is correct. The practical safeguard is a staged rollout with verification steps: configure, verify show outputs and collector ingestion, simulate failures, and monitor device performance before scaling. These practices preserve detection capability while avoiding unintended outages or noisy telemetry.

These are the essential concepts you should remember. Flexible NetFlow is a customizable telemetry system: you define flow records that specify keys and non-key fields to capture the precise traffic attributes you need for security analysis. A flow record is the schema for a flow entry; it determines which fields identify a unique flow and which values are collected as context. The flow exporter sends flow data to a NetFlow collector using a chosen transport and source interface. Keep these three concepts distinct because their separation gives you operational flexibility: reuse exporters, craft records for different security needs, and apply monitors selectively. Memorize these definitions and the operational distinction so you can design scalable telemetry with predictable resource usage. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Finish by remembering three operationally critical concepts. A flow monitor binds a record and exporter and manages an on-device cache; it is the operational object you apply to interfaces to begin collection. IP SLA operations actively probe services to measure reachability, latency, jitter, and packet loss; choose the operation type that best simulates the user experience for that service. Tracking objects convert IP SLA results into up/down states that can drive automated actions like withdrawing a static route or altering routing behavior. Together, these components let you detect threats both passively and actively and build automated responses that preserve service availability while alerts and deeper investigations proceed. The practical final takeaway is to combine focused FNF telemetry with representative IP SLA probes and to test automation in a staged manner so detection and response are reliable when they are needed most.
